title: Every LLM request is reconstructable from the session log
summary: Anything that reaches a model request must be reconstructable from the session log and the content-addressed objects it references, so anyone with the log and the same code version can rebuild every request byte for byte. Stable request prefixes for provider caching follow from this.
firstReason: Reconstructable requests give replay equivalence and provider prefix-cache hits; this is a core invariant worth keeping.

title: Initiating Agent scope over AsyncLocalStorage
summary: The agent that started an operation is carried implicitly through asynchronous calls with Node's AsyncLocalStorage, so deep infrastructure can ask which agent initiated the work without it being passed as a parameter.
firstReason: Go has no async-local storage; the same need is met by carrying the initiating agent as a value in the context.Context that every call already receives.

title: Separate context injection from turn execution
summary: inject() is the only way to add supplementary model-facing input, and a turn means exactly one execution of the model loop. Each injected context is an ordinary identified user message whose source names its producer.
firstReason: One path for injected context removes three overlapping mechanisms and keeps the log uniform; keep it.

title: Follow-up enqueue and owned run boundaries
summary: Sending a follow-up only enqueues the message and returns its id; no single message owns the activity that follows. Only high-level run() helpers return a result, defined as the last committed assistant message between the enqueue receipt and the next idle state.
firstReason: Steering, injected context and queued messages make per-message results unsound; the enqueue-only contract with explicitly owned runs should be kept in the Go SDK protocol.

title: Cancelled streams finalize their delivered prefix
summary: When a model stream is cancelled, the text the user already saw is committed as an assistant message marked interrupted, so follow-up prompts and forks include it. Tool calls in the cancelled output are left out.
firstReason: The model history must contain what the user read; the rule does not depend on the language.

title: Explicit Agent identity at runtime boundaries
summary: Agent identity is passed explicitly wherever it is needed (setup functions, event payloads, remote requests); a cordis context owns registrations and cleanup only and offers no way to look up its agent.
firstReason: Keeping lifetime ownership (the context) apart from domain identity (the agent) avoids a class of wrong-agent bugs, and explicit parameters are the Go norm.

title: Awaited per-agent initialization
summary: Agent creation runs its initialization listeners one at a time and waits for each; the agent's first model request starts only after all have finished, and a failure fails creation.
firstReason: Tools and start-up context that are installed asynchronously must be in place before the first request; keep the awaited, ordered initialization.

title: A series start with an unchanged prompt keeps the surviving system node
summary: At the start of a new request series, the system-prompt projection rewrites the first message only when the effective prompt text must move. When the latest surviving system node already holds the rendering, the nodes stay where the cached history has them, so the provider's prefix cache still hits.
firstReason: It prevents a full prompt-cache miss after a compaction or prune, which is a direct token cost. It belongs with in-history system prompt replacement, which the Go design should keep.

title: Parallel tool-call execution by per-call safety
summary: Sibling tool calls in one assistant message may run in parallel when each tool's optional `isConcurrencySafe(args)` classifier returns exactly `true`. The classifier is synchronous, pure and looks only at its own call; anything else, including a classifier that throws or invalid arguments, makes the call exclusive.
firstReason: Opt-in, per-call, fail-to-exclusive scheduling removes latency for independent reads without the scheduler having to prove anything. Goroutines make the parallel part simple; the order of log events must still be specified.

title: In-history system prompt replacement for cache-stable prompt changes
summary: For a model route that declares the capability, a changed system prompt is appended as a new system message later in the history instead of rewriting message 0, so the provider's prefix cache survives prompt changes such as entering plan mode or loading a skill.
firstReason: Every prompt change otherwise costs the whole cached prefix in a long session. The capability is declared per model, so it is a provider fact and not a JavaScript one.

title: Unify the agent id and the session id
summary: A live agent and its session share one identifier. There is no separate agent id to translate; the configuration keeps a stable label, and a fresh start mints the identifier from the label plus a random part.
firstReason: One identity for routing, event sourcing and persistence removes a mapping no production path needs. Nothing about it depends on JavaScript.

title: Remove implicit batching from ordinary sends
summary: Each call to send a message creates its own queue item and, if it runs, its own turn. Two sends are never silently combined into one turn because they happened to be waiting at the same moment, and the second turn starts only after the first has ended and its durability checkpoint has settled.
firstReason: Grouping by timing made behaviour depend on scheduling accidents. Go's goroutine scheduling would make timing-based batching even less predictable, so the explicit rule is the right one to keep.

title: One tool invocation form per agent
summary: Each agent offers its tools to the model in exactly one form: either as native function schemas, or as a single `run_code` tool with a generated SDK (programmatic tool calling, PTC). Offering both at once is rejected in configuration.
firstReason: The mixed form multiplied schema ordering, admission and test combinations without adding a capability. The rule is a configuration constraint and carries over unchanged.

title: Deterministic tests, the replay invariant fixture, and race stress
summary: Proposal: tests never sleep for a fixed time but wait for an event; after every agent-loop test the session log is replayed into a fresh session and must produce the same message history; and a nightly job repeats the loop and inbox tests many times in random order to expose races.
firstReason: Adopt all three. Replay equality is the core promise of an event-sourced session and is cheap to assert in every test, and Go's test runner already offers repetition, shuffling and a data-race detector for the stress run.
